answer.evidence: The largest volume is the stepped slope of grey brick courses, rows 16-47. It is drawn as a flat front elevation with mortar lines and a widening staircase silhouette, and none of its steps has a top plane or edge line. A tan band at rows 0-9 with a light line at row 10 could be a top, but it sits only on the narrow 14px wall stub, not on the main mass. At most 1-2 rows of lighter lip appear along the slope steps near rows 39-46. The object faces south and has no isometric side face.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate has 16 visible tones per 16x16 tile, close to the cheese stall (17) and well (20) and well above the hedge (9). Near-flat coverage is 0%, so there are no flat fills. The stone blocks are shaded one by one, with highlight, mid and shadow faces and chips on the stepped edge, which matches the reference's per-stone shading. The 100% near-neutral share of dark edge pixels follows from the stone being grey. The edges read as dark grey tones of the stone itself, not a uniform pure-black sticker line, and the forms are separated by value, so I call the outline mixed rather than near_black. The lamp reference also measures 100% neutral. The ramp is about 5 steps against the references' 5-6. It is slightly less varied than the best reference but does not look thinner or flatter beside it.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a stone rubble wall end with a stepped slope and a carved cap. Its stone blocks are shaded one by one in about 5 grey steps, from light faces to darker joints and shadow sides. That is comparable to the stone shading on the well reference. Measured density supports this: 16 visible tones per tile against 17 for the cheese stall and 20 for the well, with 0% near-flat coverage (no flat fills). The dark edge pixels are 100% near-neutral. The material is itself neutral grey stone, so a dark grey edge is close to the adjacent material's dark tone rather than a uniform black sticker line. The lamp reference has the same 100% neutral share. The outline is not clearly separated from the stone shading and mostly relies on value separation between blocks, so I call it mixed rather than fully material-toned. Overall the piece would sit next to the references without looking thinner or flatter.

answer.evidence: The whole piece is a front elevation of masonry: horizontal mortar lines at rows 15, 23, 31, 39 and 45 separate stone courses seen face-on. The stepped right-hand blocks show only 1-2 row light edges, which are rims. No horizontal surface of 3 or more rows appears anywhere, so it is front_elevation.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a grey stone wall end with a stepped slope. It reads as stone blocks with some per-block variation and has no flat fills (0% near-flat, 16 visible tones per tile, close to stall at 17 and well at 20). But the measured dark edge pixels are 100% near-neutral, and the picture agrees: the outline is a grey-black line around the whole silhouette and the block seams, not a dark tone of the stone. The references (hedge 0%, stall 1%, well 33%) carry tinted outlines. That is the sticker look. The stone ramp shows about 4 steps (light, mid, dark seam, near-black edge) against 5-6 in the references. Individual stones are shaded less than the well's stones, and the top is a pale cap with little grain. Density is acceptable, but the neutral outline and shallower ramp fall short of the Beodeul standard.
